title: Salesforce — WhatsApp-Style Web Messaging Rehearsal
briefing: A Salesforce SMTS frontend account published November 23, 2025 reports a 60-minute WhatsApp Web design round, with messaging, synchronization, offline support, and encryption considerations. Design a messaging client with conversation history, sending, delivery status, and reconnect recovery. This exercise adapts a public candidate report; company attribution and interview details are not independently verified. The practice constraints and follow-ups are Codematica additions. Use your own timer and drawing tool: 45 minutes designing, 10 minutes handling follow-ups, and 5 minutes reviewing. No coding is required. Your design is not automatically graded; reflection text is transient. The related lesson contains the source and shared rubric.
objectives: Define conversation IDs, message IDs, client operation IDs, ordering, and pending/confirmed/failed states.
Draw send → pending message → server acknowledgment → reconciliation, including a lost acknowledgment.
Distinguish server acceptance, recipient delivery, and reading. Explain deduplication, ordering, scroll preservation, and where encryption changes the client/server boundary.

prediction.prompt: Which area is most likely to expose a weakness in your first design?

options.label: An uncertain request outcome or recovery gap.
Performance or accessibility under the stated constraints.

steps.title: 0–7 minutes: clarify the scope
steps.instructions: Design a messaging client with conversation history, sending, delivery status, and reconnect recovery. Identify two main journeys, required devices, freshness, permissions, and exclusions. Separate requirements from assumptions.

steps.title: 7–20 minutes: draw the architecture
steps.instructions: Draw send → pending message → server acknowledgment → reconciliation, including a lost acknowledgment. Assign state owners and component inputs/events. Include loading, empty, and error states.

steps.title: 20–30 minutes: define data and APIs
steps.instructions: Define conversation IDs, message IDs, client operation IDs, ordering, and pending/confirmed/failed states. Specify one read and one write, including identities, response fields, cache policy, and safe retry conditions.

steps.title: 30–45 minutes: trace behavior and recovery
steps.instructions: Trace one interaction from input to confirmed state, then fail a request. Distinguish server acceptance, recipient delivery, and reading. Explain deduplication, ordering, scroll preservation, and where encryption changes the client/server boundary.

steps.title: 45–55 minutes: handle follow-ups
steps.instructions: Retry after disconnection. Open another tab. Receive duplicates. Load earlier history while new messages arrive. Pick the hardest case and show which decisions change. State any unresolved limits.

steps.title: 55–60 minutes: review your evidence
steps.instructions: Score scope, components, state and data, APIs and consistency, failure recovery, and quality and trade-offs. Use 0: missing, 1: mentioned, 2: explained with a concrete decision and consequence. Check only evidence you can show. Choose the weakest dimension and redraw it; this is not an employer hiring threshold.

evidenceChecklist.label: I stated the main journeys, assumptions, and exclusions.
I drew component responsibilities and interaction contracts.
I assigned state owners, stable identities, and invariants.
I defined reads, writes, caching, and reconciliation.
I traced one failure through usable recovery.
I defended accessibility, performance, measurement, and alternatives.
I distinguished acceptance, delivery, and reading, and traced a lost acknowledgment without duplicate messages.

reflectionPrompts: Distinguish server acceptance, recipient delivery, and reading. Explain deduplication, ordering, scroll preservation, and where encryption changes the client/server boundary.
Which decision changed after a follow-up, and what requirement caused it?
Which dimension was weakest, and what will you redraw next time?
extensionChallenge: Add another device and offline sending. Explain deduplication and encrypted-history synchronization without assuming the server can read message contents.
